probes.query: I discarded a long stretch of old operation history and then ran the storage-cleanup command with its expiry set to the present moment. Trace how commits that only the discarded history referenced end up deleted from the underlying Git store. Cover: how the discard step changes the stored history so that the commit index forgets those commits, which operation and view records the cleanup keeps, how the set of surviving commits is derived and pinned against Git's own pruning, and how Git's pruning is finally run and with what cutoff.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The discard step (cmd_op_abandon) calls op_walk::reparent_range, which writes copies of every descendant operation with rewritten parent lists (attached to the destination operation), so those operations get new operation IDs and the old ones become unreachable.

CRITICAL: The default index store keys its saved index by operation ID (op_links directory). The new head operation has no saved link, so get_index_at_op falls back to build_index_at_operation, which starts from the nearest ancestor operation that has a link (for example the root operation) and indexes only commits referenced by the surviving operations, so commits referenced only by discarded operations are never re-indexed.

build_index_at_operation collects heads from Operation::all_referenced_commit_ids (which includes the predecessor commits recorded by the operation) plus each operation's View::all_referenced_commit_ids.

The cleanup command (cmd_util_gc) requires the head operation, uses a two-week cutoff by default (only the value 'now' is accepted to override), and calls the operation store's gc with the current operation as the only head, then GitBackend::gc with the current index.

SimpleOpStore::gc walks operations depth-first from the head to find reachable operations and their views, then deletes operation and view files that are not reachable unless their modification time is newer than the cutoff.

GitBackend::gc takes index.all_heads_for_gc() (heads of all indexed commits, excluding the root commit), rewrites the refs under refs/jj/keep/<commit id> via recreate_no_gc_refs (deleting other keep refs unless the loose ref is newer than the cutoff), garbage-collects the extra-metadata table segments, and then runs git gc through the configured Git executable with a prune cutoff of the form @<unix seconds> +0000.

probes.query: I turned on commit signing in my configuration but never run any dedicated signing command. Trace how a commit that jj writes or rewrites ends up carrying a cryptographic signature inside the Git object. Cover: which rule decides whether a given commit gets signed (and how that changes when someone else authored it or it was already signed), how the signing program is chosen among the supported ones, how the signing key is picked when none is given for the GPG family versus SSH, where in the Git commit the signature is stored, and how pushing treats commits that are not signed yet.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: SignSettings::should_sign (settings.rs) decides per commit from the configured behavior: drop never signs; keep signs only if the commit already has a signature and its author email equals the user email; own signs whenever the author email equals the user email; force always signs. The default behavior is keep and the default backend is none (lib/src/config/misc.toml).

CRITICAL: commit_builder::write_to_store signs only if store.signer().can_sign() (a main backend is configured) and should_sign is true; it clears the commit's old secure_sig and passes a signing closure (Signer::sign with an optional per-commit key override) into Store::write_commit.

The Signer is built when the repo loader is initialized from the file system (RepoLoader::init_from_file_system in repo.rs calls signing_factory::signer_from_settings): it instantiates the GPG, GPGSM and SSH backends (plus a test one), picks the main backend by the configured backend name (none means no main backend, an unknown name is an error), and keeps the others only for verification.

Default key when no override is given: GPG uses the configured signing key, falling back to the user email; GPGSM always falls back to the user email; SSH uses the configured signing key and returns a MissingKey error if there is none.

GitBackend::write_commit serializes the commit, calls the signing closure on those bytes, and stores the signature as an extra commit header whose name depends on the Git hash kind (signature_field_name), and keeps the signed data in the commit's secure signature.

On push, when the sign-on-push setting is on (default false), sign_commits_before_push forces the 'own' behavior, signs only mutable unsigned commits authored by the user (reparenting descendants and remapping the pushed ref updates), and warns about immutable commits that need a signature but are skipped.

probes.query: A local bookmark follows a branch on a remote only once that remote branch is marked as tracked. Apart from running the explicit command that starts tracking, in which situations does jj mark a remote branch as tracked by itself? Name each situation, the setting (if there is one) that controls it, and the function that makes the decision.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: When Git refs are imported (fetch, import, colocated sync), a remote bookmark seen for the first time starts tracked only if its remote is the internal local-Git pseudo-remote or its name matches that remote's configured auto-track matcher, otherwise it starts untracked; tags always start tracked. This is default_remote_ref_state_for (lib/git.rs), fed by GitImportOptions.remote_auto_track_bookmarks, which load_git_import_options builds with parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map from the per-remote settings (RemoteSettings).

CRITICAL: Creating a bookmark, or setting one that is new, starts tracking it on every remote whose matcher matches its name, where the matcher is the union of the auto-track-bookmarks and auto-track-created-bookmarks expressions (parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map_for_new_bookmarks) and tracking uses MutableRepo::track_remote_bookmark; a warning is printed if the bookmark already exists on that remote.

When cloning, the remote's default branch is tracked, but only if the chosen working branch is the default branch and the Git setting for tracking the default bookmark on clone is on (default true in misc.toml).
Exporting local bookmarks to Git records them in the view as tracked entries of the internal Git pseudo-remote (copy_exportable_local_bookmarks_to_remote_view in lib/git.rs).
After a successful push, push_refs records each pushed bookmark and tag in the remote view with state Tracked.

Renaming a bookmark carries tracking over: for each remote where the old bookmark was tracked, the new name is tracked, unless an untracked remote bookmark with the new name already exists (a warning is printed and tracking is dropped).

probes.query: A GraphQL schema author marks a list-of-decimals field as a stored vector and asks for nearest-neighbour search on it, writing the search option text so that it sets only the one tuning value that controls how quickly the number of graph layers scales. Follow that option text from the GraphQL schema to the point where an index object exists. Which step first rejects an unknown option name or an unsupported distance-measure name, how does the engine find the index implementation from its name, and what values do the layer-count, build-effort, search-effort and distance-measure settings take when they are left out?

graphql/schema/schemagen.go getAllSearchIndexes appends the rewritten options to the index name, the embedding field gets the Dgraph type float32vector, and the generated Dgraph schema line prints the index as @index(<name>(<options>)).

The admin schema-update resolver (graphql/admin/schema.go) passes the generated Dgraph schema (DGSchema) to edgraph.UpdateGQLSchema, which runs parseSchemaFromAlterOperation (schema.ParseWithNamespace) in the Alpha before any proposal reaches the cluster.

CRITICAL: Defaults are applied when the index object is created (FactoryCreateSpec.CreateIndex -> CreateOrReplace -> persistentHNSW.applyOptions): if exponent is given, any missing maxLevels = exponent, efConstruction = 50 x exponent and efSearch = 30 x exponent; with nothing given the values are 3, 150 and 90; a missing metric means euclidean.

probes.query: An operator changes the definition of an existing field that already holds data, for example switching its search indexing, its reverse-direction or counting support, or making it multi-valued. Which kinds of change make the server delete and rebuild stored derived data, which only delete it, and which are refused or need nothing? While the background rebuild runs, which definition of the field do ordinary reads see compared with incoming writes, what happens to another definition-change request that arrives meanwhile, and what else on the server changes behaviour?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: posting/index.go IndexRebuild decides per aspect. Search index: no index before or after means nothing; index removed means delete only; value type changed means delete everything and rebuild; otherwise the tokenizer sets (and vector index specs by name plus options) are diffed, deleting removed ones and rebuilding added ones. Reverse and count: turned on means rebuild, turned off means delete, unchanged means nothing. NeedIndexRebuild is true if any of the three says rebuild.

Scalar to list is a data rewrite run first (BuildData -> rebuildListType re-keys the untagged value by fingerprint); list to scalar is refused (needsListTypeRebuild error, and checkSchema in worker/mutation.go refuses it when edges exist), as are scalar-uid changes while data exists and password type changes.

CRITICAL: While rebuilding, schema.State has two views: reads see the 'query schema' from GetQuerySchema (new definition minus tokenizers pending deletion, with count and reverse switched off while they rebuild), while writes (IsWrite context) see the new definition stored with SetMutSchema; the mutation entry is cleared when done and the old schema restored on failure (undoSchemaUpdate).

runSchemaMutation (worker/mutation.go) starts the rebuild as the opIndexing task (cancelling the rollup task), runs one goroutine per predicate throttled by a Badger-file-based limit, and the leader proposes a snapshot afterwards if the work took at least ten seconds; other group members block in waitForTask(opIndexing) until it finishes.

Another alter request is rejected by edgraph parseSchemaFromAlterOperation with errIndexingInProgress as long as any mutation schema exists (state.IndexingInProgress); Alter sleeps one second before returning so the client waits.
While indexing is in progress posting/list.go skips the fast length shortcut in getPostingAndLengthNoSort and uses the slow path.

probes.query: A monorepo is documented one package at a time and the per-package results are combined afterwards. Package A's public API mentions a class declared in package B. While A is being documented, the compiler sees B only through its compiled declaration files, which carry source maps back to B's TypeScript. expectedFacts: Converting a type mention creates an unresolved ReferenceType that carries a ReflectionSymbolId (referenceConverter -> Context.createSymbolReference -> createSymbolId -> createSymbolIdImpl), not a pointer to a reflection, because B is not part of A's project.

CRITICAL: The identity is package name + package-relative path + qualified name. The path part comes from the original source file found by mapping the compiled declaration file through resolveDeclarationMaps (it reads the sibling .map file, takes the first of its sources joined with any source root). The mapping cache is pre-filled by addInferredDeclarationMapPaths, called from getEntryPrograms for the root program and every referenced project, so the identity does not depend on where compiled output lives. The package name is taken from findPackageForPath on the unmapped declaration-file path.

When saving, ReferenceType.toObject writes the numeric reflection id only if the target resolves inside the same project; otherwise it writes symbolId.toObject(), which keeps only package name, package path and qualified name (position and transient id are dropped). ProjectReflection.toObject also writes a symbolIdMap of its own reflections.

Application._convertPackages serializes each package project (serializer.projectToObject) and then calls Deserializer.reviveProjects, which revives each project as a module under one combined project. Each saved symbolIdMap is re-registered in a deferred step (de.defer) after oldIdToNewId is filled - in DeclarationReflection.fromObject for the project-variant branch used when merging, not in ProjectReflection.fromObject - and ReferenceType.fromObject rebuilds a ReflectionSymbolId and points the reference at the combined project.

CRITICAL: ProjectReflection keeps symbolToReflectionIdMap as a StableKeyMap keyed by ReflectionSymbolId.getStableKey(), which omits position and transient id when position is not finite (as for deserialized ids). A's deserialized reference and B's deserialized registration therefore share the key packageName/packagePath/qualifiedName, and the lazy ReferenceType.reflection getter resolves it through getReflectionsFromSymbolId, preferring type-like or value-like kinds according to preferValues.

On the page, formatter.tsx's reference handler uses type.reflection: when it resolves it renders each segment of getUniquePath as an anchor if router.hasUrl(item) (href from urlTo) and as a plain span otherwise; if it does not resolve it falls back to externalUrl or the bare name.

probes.query: My project has two entry modules which I listed in a deliberate order, one of which also has markdown documents attached, and nothing about ordering is configured. In what order do the modules appear in the sidebar and on the index page, in what order are the members of a class listed within its page, and in what order do the page's sections appear (give the English names of the first three sections on a module page that has documents, classes and functions)? Documents therefore come first and are never alphabetized, so they keep their original order.

Sections (groups) are not ordered by that comparator: GroupPlugin.sortGroupCallback orders them by weights, which by default are the plural kind names in a fixed order (Documents, Modules, Namespaces, ... - so a module page with documents, classes and functions shows Documents, Classes, Functions in that order); a group-order setting replaces the list and '*' marks where unlisted names go, otherwise unlisted names come last, ties broken alphabetically. When categories exist they are the sections instead (or are nested as 'group - category' when categorize-by-group is on) and are ordered by their own order setting with the same wildcard rule; CategoryPlugin re-sorts each category's children with the same comparator.

CRITICAL: GroupPlugin.group sorts a container's children, documents and combined list only when the keep-entry-order setting is on (default true) or none of its children is a module; so by default modules are sorted alphabetically by name, and when the setting is turned off a container whose children are modules keeps the order in which entry points (or modules) were created and its documents are left unsorted too.

A comment tag naming a strategy on the container replaces the default list for that container only. GroupPlugin.getSortFunction splits the text on commas/whitespace, warns for each invalid name and passes only the valid ones; CategoryPlugin silently drops invalid names. probes.query: Operators can relax the exact matching of trace identifiers, so that a 128-bit identifier and its lower 64-bit half count as the same trace. CRITICAL: Cassandra changes the stored layout when relaxed: InsertSpan.Factory.newInput splits a 32-character id into trace_id_high (first 16) and trace_id (last 16), and InsertTraceByServiceSpan and InsertTraceByServiceRemoteService index only the lower 16 characters; SelectFromSpan.Factory.newCall queries both the full and the lower id when relaxed and filters (StrictTraceId.filterSpans or filterTraces) when exact, and SelectSpansByTraceIds applies FilterTraces only when exact.

probes.query: An operator submits a complete replacement settings document to the gateway's runtime administration interface, and the document fails validation. expectedFacts: FileConfigurationController.Post calls IFileConfigurationSetter.SetAsync and, on any exception, returns BadRequest with e.ToShortString(), the format "TypeName: all inner messages".

CRITICAL: FileAndInternalConfigurationSetter.SetAsync first persists through IFileConfigurationRepository.SetAsync and only afterwards builds the internal configuration; if creation reports errors it throws ConfigurationRepositoryException and never calls AddOrReplace.

CRITICAL: DiskFileConfigurationRepository.SetAsync deletes and rewrites the environment-specific file and then the primary ocelot.json, then activates the change-token source, all before validation; so the invalid document stays on disk and the signal is raised once, while the live in-memory configuration stays unchanged.

probes.query: The DNS-over-HTTPS resolver keeps its own cache of answers, separate from the application's HTTP response cache. How long is an answer served, when does it get refreshed, how are failures and empty answers cached, and which record types share entries? Also say what bounds the number of entries and what decides which ones are evicted, and whether the operating system's default resolver goes through this cache. expectedFacts: The public DnsCache defaults are minimum TTL 10 s, maximum TTL 300 s, failure TTL 10 s, revalidate-before-expire 2 s and 1000 entries; it wraps a RealDnsCache and is used only by DnsOverHttps (Builder default DnsCache(); queryFactory = cache.-delegate.wrap(DnsOverHttpsQuery.Factory)); the default system resolver (Dns.SYSTEM, InetAddressDns) never goes through it.

CRITICAL: Entries are keyed by the DNS Question (name, type, class), so A, AAAA and HTTPS (service metadata) answers are cached separately; DnsOverHttps.newCall builds StateMachineDnsCall, which asks HTTPS (when includeServiceMetadata, with the _port._https. name for a non-443 port), AAAA (when includeIPv6) and A, while DnsOverHttps.lookup runs a copy with includeServiceMetadata = false that shares the same cache.

CRITICAL: RealDnsCache.CacheQuery.onResponse sets the lifetime to the minimum answer TTL (seconds) coerced into [minimumTimeToLive, maximumTimeToLive], or to failureTimeToLive when the response has no answers; revalidateAt = sentAt + max(0, lifetime - revalidateBeforeExpire) and expireAt = sentAt + lifetime. onFailure stores a Failure result for failureTimeToLive and replays that exception to queries until it expires.

CacheQuery.enqueue serves the stored result while now < expireAt, and starts a new network query when there is no result or now >= revalidateAt (so within the last revalidate window a still-valid answer is returned immediately while a refresh runs in the background); if the result is expired and a query is already in flight, the caller joins that in-flight call; cancelling a CacheQuery does not cancel the network query, so the cache is still updated.

MemoryCache.computeIfAbsent never evicts until the entry count reaches twice maxSize and then evicts down to maxSize in one batch (maxSize 0 disables caching: a new Entry each time and nothing stored); RealDnsCache.lastRequestedAt returns null for entries that are expired with no in-flight call (evicted unconditionally) and otherwise the last request time, and MemoryCache.evict removes the least recently requested using a priority queue that drops the newest.

Does the library rebuild or tidy the presented certificate chain while it sets up the connection? One statement is executing on it and two more statements are queued behind it on the same transaction. The executing statement fails on the server. expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Database.clearSchemaCacheIfNeeded compares PRAGMA schema_version (the 4-byte counter in the file header) with lastSchemaVersion and calls clearSchemaCache only when it changed.

CRITICAL: DatabasePool calls it on the reader connection at the start of every read flavour: read (sync and async variants), asyncRead, unsafeRead (sync and async), asyncUnsafeRead, unsafeReentrantRead (when it takes a pooled reader), and the concurrent-read start, where the same call doubles as the first SELECT that establishes snapshot isolation. WALSnapshotTransaction.init does it right after BEGIN DEFERRED.

On the connection that runs the change itself (the writer), staleness is detected per statement: StatementAuthorizer sets invalidatesDatabaseSchemaCache for DROP, CREATE, ALTER, ATTACH and DETACH action codes, and for the internal drop-column function on SQLite older than 3.38; Database.statementDidExecute then calls clearSchemaCache.
Database.withSchemaSource clears the cache both before running its block and after it (in defer), so information loaded through either schema source does not linger.
Database.backupInternal clears the schema cache of the destination connection when the copy finishes.
clearSchemaCache also empties the internal and public prepared-statement caches, because automatic statement recompilation is limited in the number of retries.
